Modules can be pushed to and executed by Duqu that copy data to a staging area, compress it, and XOR encrypt it.
Duqu uses a custom command and control protocol that communicates over commonly used ports, and is frequently encapsulated by application layer protocols.
The reconnaissance modules used with Duqu can collect information on network configuration.
Adversaries can instruct Duqu to spread laterally by copying itself to shares it has enumerated and for which it has obtained legitimate credentials (via keylogging or other means). The remote host is then infected by using the compromised credentials to schedule a task on remote machines that executes the malware.
Duqu can track key presses with a keylogger module.
Duqu can be configured to have commands relayed over a peer-to-peer network of infected hosts if some of the hosts do not have Internet access.
Duqu creates a new service that loads a malicious driver when the system starts. When Duqu is active, the operating system believes that the driver is legitimate, as it has been signed with a valid private key.
Duqu will inject itself into different processes to evade detection. The selection of the target process is influenced by the security software that is installed on the system (Duqu will inject into different processes depending on which security suite is installed on the infected host).
Duqu is capable of loading executable code via process hollowing.
The discovery modules used with Duqu can collect information on open windows.
The Duqu command and control protocol's data stream can be encrypted with AES-CBC.
The discovery modules used with Duqu can collect information on network connections.
The discovery modules used with Duqu can collect information on accounts and permissions.
When the Duqu command and control is operating over HTTP or HTTPS, Duqu uploads data to its controller by appending it to a blank JPG file.
ref-033d040ec33958a8b08a.title: Symantec Security Response. (2011, November). W32.Duqu: The precursor to the next Stuxnet. Retrieved September 17, 2015.

ref-1294dab4884a168e2164.text: OopsIE has the capability to delete files and scripts from the victim's machine. OopsIE checks to see if the system is configured with "Daylight" time and checks for a specific region to be set for the timezone. OopsIE performs several anti-VM and sandbox checks on the victim's machine. One technique the group has used was to perform a WMI query SELECT * FROM MSAcpi_ThermalZoneTemperature to check the temperature to see if it’s running in a virtual environment. OopsIE uses WMI to perform discovery techniques. OopsIE checks for information on the CPU fan, temperature, mouse, hard disk, and motherboard as part of its anti-VM checks.
ref-1294dab4884a168e2164.title: Falcone, R., et al. (2018, September 04). OilRig Targets a Middle Eastern Government and Adds Evasion Techniques to OopsIE. Retrieved September 24, 2018.

ref-5853719c4df0411df2c6.text:
TrickBot can identify the groups the user on a compromised host belongs to.
TrickBot has come with a signed downloader component.
Anchor has obfuscated code with stack strings and string encryption.
TrickBot uses HTTPS to communicate with its C2 servers, to get malware updates, modules that perform most of the malware logic and various configuration files.
Anchor can self delete its dropper after the malware is successfully deployed.
Anchor can use secondary C2 servers for communication after establishing connectivity and relaying victim information to primary C2 servers.
TrickBot can enumerate computers and network devices.
TrickBot has been delivered via malicious links in phishing e-mails.
Anchor has used HTTP and HTTPS in C2 communications.
TrickBot can gather information about domain trusts by utilizing Nltest.
TrickBot decodes the configuration data and modules.
Anchor can establish persistence by creating a service.
Anchor has used ICMP in C2 communications.
Anchor has used NTFS to hide files.
Anchor can terminate itself if specific execution flags are not present.
Cobalt Strike can determine if the user on an infected machine is in the admin or domain admin group.
Anchor has come with a packed payload.
TrickBot can identify the user and groups the user belongs to on a compromised host.
TrickBot can steal passwords from the KeePass open source password manager.
Anchor can create a scheduled task for persistence.
TrickBot injects into the svchost.exe process.
The TrickBot downloader has used an icon to appear as a Microsoft Word document.
TrickBot can Base64-encode C2 commands.
TrickBot can use secondary C2 servers for communication after establishing connectivity and relaying victim information to primary C2 servers.
Anchor has used cmd.exe to run its self deletion routine.
Anchor has been signed with valid certificates to evade detection by security tools.
ref-5853719c4df0411df2c6.title: Dahan, A. et al. (2019, December 11). DROPPING ANCHOR: FROM A TRICKBOT INFECTION TO THE DISCOVERY OF THE ANCHOR MALWARE. Retrieved September 10, 2020.

ref-589c605e1fd4470ec80a.text: Comnie executes the netstat -ano command. Comnie appends a total of 64MB of garbage data to a file to deter any security products in place that may be scanning files on disk. Comnie collects the hostname of the victim machine. Comnie attempts to detect several anti-virus products. Comnie uses HTTP for C2 communication. Comnie establishes persistence via a .lnk file in the victim’s startup path. Comnie uses RC4 and Base64 to obfuscate strings. Comnie encrypts command and control communications with RC4. Comnie runs the command: net start >> %TEMP%\info.dat on a victim. Comnie executes BAT scripts. Comnie executes a batch script to store discovery information in %TEMP%\info.dat and then uploads the temporarily file to the remote C2 server. Comnie uses the net user command. Comnie achieves persistence by adding a shortcut of itself to the startup path in the Registry. Comnie uses the tasklist to view running processes on the victim’s machine. Comnie executes VBS scripts. Comnie uses Rundll32 to load a malicious DLL. Comnie uses ipconfig /all and route PRINT to identify network adapter and interface information. Comnie uses blogs and third-party sites (GitHub, tumbler, and BlogSpot) to avoid DNS-based blocking of their communication to the command and control server.
ref-589c605e1fd4470ec80a.title: Grunzweig, J. (2018, January 31). Comnie Continues to Target Organizations in East Asia. Retrieved June 7, 2018.

ref-5e874bf3ddef27a8e97c.text: NavRAT leverages cmd.exe to perform discovery techniques. NavRAT loads malicious shellcode and executes it in memory. NavRAT uses tasklist /v to check running processes. NavRAT writes multiple outputs to a TMP file using the >> method. NavRAT uses systeminfo on a victim’s machine. NavRAT can download files remotely. NavRAT creates a Registry key to ensure a file gets executed upon reboot in order to establish persistence. NavRAT uses the email platform, Naver, for C2 communications, leveraging SMTP. NavRAT logs the keystrokes on the targeted system. NavRAT copies itself into a running Internet Explorer process to evade detection.
ref-5e874bf3ddef27a8e97c.title: Mercer, W., Rascagneres, P. (2018, May 31). NavRAT Uses US-North Korea Summit As Decoy For Attacks In South Korea. Retrieved June 11, 2018.

ref-621016e6eff85e96bd72.text: RogueRobin uses a command prompt to run a PowerShell script from Excel. To assist in establishing persistence, RogueRobin creates %APPDATA%\OneDrive.bat and saves the following string to it:powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden -exec bypass -File “%APPDATA%\OneDrive.ps1”. RogueRobin uses WMI to check BIOS version for VBOX, bochs, qemu, virtualbox, and vm to check for evidence that the script might be executing within an analysis environment. RogueRobin uses Windows Script Components. RogueRobin uses various WMI queries to check if the sample is running in a sandbox. RogueRobin gathers BIOS versions and manufacturers, the number of CPU cores, the total physical memory, and the computer name. RogueRobin can save a new file to the system from the C2 server. RogueRobin created a shortcut in the Windows startup folder to launch a PowerShell script each time the user logs in to establish persistence. RogueRobin establishes persistence by creating a shortcut (.LNK file) in the Windows startup folder to run a script each time the user logs in. RogueRobin checks the running processes for evidence it may be running in a sandbox environment. It specifically enumerates processes for Wireshark and Sysinternals. RogueRobin has a command named $screenshot that may be responsible for taking screenshots of the victim machine. RogueRobin collects the victim’s username and whether that user is an admin. RogueRobin enumerates running processes to search for Wireshark and Windows Sysinternals suite. RogueRobin gathers the IP address and domain from the victim’s machine. RogueRobin base64 encodes strings that are sent to the C2 over its DNS tunnel.
ref-621016e6eff85e96bd72.title: Falcone, R., et al. (2018, July 27). New Threat Actor Group DarkHydrus Targets Middle East Government. Retrieved August 2, 2018.

ref-624de41e7fa70a8cc616.text: TAINTEDSCRIBE can copy itself into the current user’s Startup folder as “Narrator.exe” for persistence. TAINTEDSCRIBE can download additional modules from its C2 server. TAINTEDSCRIBE can use DriveList to retrieve drive information. TAINTEDSCRIBE has used FakeTLS for session authentication. TAINTEDSCRIBE can randomly pick one of five hard-coded IP addresses for C2 communication; if one of the IP fails, it will wait 60 seconds and then try another IP address. TAINTEDSCRIBE can execute FileRecvWriteRand to append random bytes to the end of a file received from C2. TAINTEDSCRIBE uses a Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR) algorithm for network encryption. The TAINTEDSCRIBE main executable has disguised itself as Microsoft’s Narrator. TAINTEDSCRIBE can execute ProcessList for process discovery. TAINTEDSCRIBE can execute GetLocalTime for time discovery. TAINTEDSCRIBE can delete files from a compromised host. TAINTEDSCRIBE has used FileReadZipSend to compress a file and send to C2. TAINTEDSCRIBE can enable Windows CLI access and execute files. The TAINTEDSCRIBE command and execution module can perform target system enumeration. TAINTEDSCRIBE can change the timestamp of specified filenames. TAINTEDSCRIBE can use DirectoryList to enumerate files in a specified directory.
ref-624de41e7fa70a8cc616.title: USG. (2020, May 12). MAR-10288834-2.v1 – North Korean Trojan: TAINTEDSCRIBE. Retrieved March 5, 2021.

ref-76847ae693931dda509f.text:
TrickBot module shareDll/mshareDll discovers network shares via the WNetOpenEnumA API.
TrickBot uses brute-force attack against RDP with rdpscanDll module.
TrickBot uses vncDll module to remote control the victim machine.
TrickBot uses module networkDll for process list discovery.
ref-76847ae693931dda509f.title: Tudorica, R., Maximciuc, A., Vatamanu, C. (2020, March 18). New TrickBot Module Bruteforces RDP Connections, Targets Select Telecommunication Services in US and Hong Kong. Retrieved March 15, 2021.

ref-7f934ddfef88cb2996c1.text: QakBot can capture keystrokes on a compromised host. QakBot has the ability to use HTTP and HTTPS in communication with C2 servers. QakBot can Base64 encode system information sent to C2. QakBot can run nltest /domain_trusts /all_trusts for domain trust discovery. QakBot can conduct brute force attacks to capture credentials. QakBot can execute WMI queries to gather information. QakBot can RC4 encrypt strings in C2 communication. QakBot can identify the system time on a targeted host. The QakBot proxy module can encapsulate SOCKS5 protocol within its own proxy protocol. QakBot can inject itself into processes including explore.exe, Iexplore.exe, Mobsync.exe., and wermgr.exe. QakBot can use net localgroup to enable discovery of local groups. QakBot has the ability use TCP to send or receive C2 packets. The QakBot web inject module can inject Java Script into web banking pages visited by the victim. QakBot can identify the user name on a compromised system. QakBot can measure the download speed on a targeted host. QakBot can use net config workstation, arp -a, `nslookup`, and ipconfig /all to gather network configuration information. QakBot can use netstat to enumerate current network connections. QakBot can identify remote systems through the net view command. QakBot has a module that can proxy C2 communications. QakBot can use net share to identify network shares for use in lateral movement. QakBot can target and steal locally stored emails to support thread hijacking phishing campaigns. QakBot can send stolen information to C2 nodes including passwords, accounts, and emails. QakBot has collected usernames and passwords from Firefox and Chrome. QakBot has the ability to capture web session cookies.
ref-7f934ddfef88cb2996c1.title: Kuzmenko, A. et al. (2021, September 2). QakBot technical analysis. Retrieved September 27, 2021.

ref-a870c046e54be33af100.text:
QUADAGENT was likely obfuscated using `Invoke-Obfuscation`.
The PowerShell script with the RogueRobin payload was obfuscated using the COMPRESS technique in `Invoke-Obfuscation`.
ref-a870c046e54be33af100.title: Bohannon, D.. (2017, March 13). Invoke-Obfuscation - PowerShell Obfuscator. Retrieved June 18, 2017.

ref-f2dd3e5584596d6ea27a.text: Gold Dragon collects endpoint information using the systeminfo command. RunningRAT captures keystrokes and sends them back to the C2 server. RunningRAT contains code to compress files. Gold Dragon collects the endpoint victim's username and uses it as a basis for downloading additional components from the C2 server. Brave Prince gathers file and directory information from the victim’s machine. Gold Dragon stores information gathered from the endpoint in a file named 1.hwp. Gold Dragon can download additional components from the C2 server. Some Brave Prince variants have used South Korea's Daum email service to exfiltrate information, and later variants have posted the data to a web server via an HTTP post command. Brave Prince lists the running processes. RunningRAT kills antimalware running process. Gold Dragon encrypts data using Base64 before being sent to the command and control server. Gold Dragon checks for anti-malware products and processes. RunningRAT contains code to delete files from the victim’s machine. Gold Dragon establishes persistence in the Startup folder. Brave Prince terminates antimalware processes. RunningRAT contains code to open and copy data from the clipboard. Gold Dragon uses cmd.exe to execute commands for discovery. RunningRAT contains code to clear event logs. RunningRAT gathers logical drives information and volume information. Gold Dragon enumerates registry keys with the command regkeyenum and obtains information for the Registry key HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Gold Dragon terminates anti-malware processes if they’re found running on the system. RunningRAT uses a batch file to kill a security program task and then attempts to remove itself. Brave Prince collects hard drive content and system configuration information. RunningRAT gathers the OS version and processor information. Gold Dragon uses HTTP for communication to the control servers. Gold Dragon lists the directories for Desktop, program files, and the user’s recently accessed files. Brave Prince gathers network configuration information as well as the ARP cache. RunningRAT adds itself to the Registry key Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run to establish persistence upon reboot. Gold Dragon checks the running processes on the victim’s machine. Brave Prince gathers information about the Registry. Gold Dragon deletes one of its files, 2.hwp, from the endpoint after establishing persistence.
ref-f2dd3e5584596d6ea27a.title: Sherstobitoff, R., Saavedra-Morales, J. (2018, February 02). Gold Dragon Widens Olympics Malware Attacks, Gains Permanent Presence on Victims’ Systems. Retrieved June 6, 2018.

ref-f8505516f734c9e6b241.text:
RogueRobin uses regsvr32.exe to run a .sct file for execution.
RogueRobin decodes an embedded executable using base64 and decompresses it.
RogueRobin has used Google Drive as a Command and Control channel.
ref-f8505516f734c9e6b241.title: Lee, B., Falcone, R. (2019, January 18). DarkHydrus delivers new Trojan that can use Google Drive for C2 communications. Retrieved April 17, 2019.
